power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Despite growing interest in advanced meditation, the cognitive mechanisms underlying these capacities remain poorly understood.
This paper develops a cognitive account of advanced meditation as a specialized form of metacognitive skill learning.
Drawing on classic accounts of skill acquisition, we propose the automatization of metacognitive control as a mechanism through which meditative skill develops.
Through sustained practice, practitioners become less reliant on explicit instructions as metacognitive control becomes increasingly automatic.
This shift may allow meditative practice to become more effective, fluent, and less effortful.
The resulting metacognitive control is directed toward well-defined phenomenological targets, including advanced absorption states and insight stages.
By connecting cognitive mechanisms with neural findings and experiential descriptions, the account offers a testable framework for explaining the development of advanced meditative capacities.

Meditation research has built a substantial body of evidence regarding the neural and experiential changes associated with meditative practice, as well as its beneficial effects on psychological well-being.

While this research has identified many important components and outcomes of meditation, comparatively little is known about how meditative capacities are acquired, stabilized, and integrated (Grabovac et al., 2026).

text.text: Building on this foundation, this paper proposes that advanced meditation can be understood as a specialized domain of metacognitive skill.

We draw on classic models of perceptual-motor skill and cognitive skill acquisition (Anderson, 1982; Fitts, 1964), as well as recent work on metacognitive skill and mindfulness development (Conway-Smith, 2025; Kee, 2019), to examine automatization as a candidate mechanism of meditative skill acquisition.

text.text: We propose that meditative development involves a transition from metacognitive control guided by explicit declarative knowledge toward increasingly implicit procedural operations.
Through repeated practice, deliberate mental actions become more effective, stable, and automatic while requiring less conscious effort.

Earlier cognitive accounts identified regulatory skills involved in meditation and described how their use changes with training. Lutz et al. (2008) characterized focused attention practice in terms of monitoring for distraction, disengaging from it, and redirecting attention, with extensive practice reducing the need for effortful regulation.

text.text: Building on this account, we propose a learning mechanism through which instruction-guided regulation becomes increasingly automatic: repeated practice embeds explicit directions within condition-action procedures, reducing the need to retrieve and deliberately apply instructions.
We examine how this transition may support the stabilization of advanced concentration and the integration of insight while preserving higher-level strategic control.
Our proposal builds on Sparby et al. (2026), who define advanced meditation in terms of states, stages, and endpoints arising through the maturation and mastery of awareness skills.

Ehmann et al. (2025) complement this account by identifying training variables, including volume, intensity, frequency, and periodization, that may shape this development.

(2025)</ref> complement this account by identifying training variables, including volume, intensity, frequency, and periodization, that may shape this development.

text.text: Together, these frameworks specify the developmental transition and training conditions to which the proposed skill learning mechanism applies.

This mechanism may contribute to the development and stabilization of several advanced meditative capacities, including those cultivated through advanced concentrative absorption meditation (ACAM; Sparby & Sacchet, 2024) and advanced investigative insight meditation (AIIM; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b), as well as progression through the stages of the Insight Development Process (IDP; Grabovac et al., 2026).

text.text: Metacognitive skill learning may also help explain culminating events and persistent changes associated with meditative endpoints (MEND; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025a).

text.text: The account proposed here does not endorse a strong automaticity view of meditative or metacognitive skill.
A comprehensive skill theory must also explain characteristics of expertise such as higher-level strategic control, affect regulation, metacontrol, and flexibility.

As, to our knowledge, this is the first attempt to integrate research on metacognitive skill with advanced meditation, we will focus on a particular learning mechanism rather than offering a complete theory of meditative expertise.
Automatization therefore provides a starting point for this account, while we also consider how it interacts with higher-level control and flexibility.

Because this account connects advanced meditative experience with the cognitive mechanisms through which it develops, it spans multiple levels of analysis. Marr (1982) developed a multilevel framework for understanding biological and artificial cognitive systems, distinguishing between the implementation, algorithmic/representational, and computational levels of explanation.

text.text: Inspired by this framework, Figure 1 organizes the proposed account across three complementary levels.
text.formatted: Inspired by this framework, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> organizes the proposed account across three complementary levels.

text.text: The neural level concerns the biological mechanisms through which meditative processes are implemented, the cognitive level concerns the representations and information-processing operations involved, and the experiential level (or phenomenological level) concerns the structure and qualities of conscious experience.
These levels connect the neural and cognitive mechanisms of automatization to changes in meditative experience.

By grounding advanced meditation in theories of metacognition and skill acquisition and connecting these processes to well-defined experiential targets, this paper offers a testable cognitive framework for understanding how meditative training produces stable, transformative states and capacities.
The relationship between advanced meditation and metacognitive skill may in turn be mutually informative.

Metacognitive skill acquisition offers a framework for explaining aspects of meditative development, while meditation provides a particularly rich domain for investigating how metacognitive skills are acquired.
More broadly, this work provides a theoretical basis for understanding how human cognition can skillfully regulate its own processes in ways that support psychological well-being.

Metacognition refers to the broad capacity of human cognition to monitor and control its own processes (Flavell, 1979). Nelson and Narens (1990) helped formalize this distinction by separating the object-level, where cognitive activity occurs, from the meta-level, which monitors and controls that activity.

text.text: This capacity encompasses the monitoring and control of processes such as emotion, reasoning, memory, and attention (Fleming & Dolan, 2012; Proust, 2013).
text.formatted: This capacity encompasses the monitoring and control of processes such as emotion, reasoning, memory, and attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fleming & Dolan, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Proust, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Metacognition can include processes that operate through implicit, non-conceptual signals such as feelings of knowing, fluency, and confidence (Koriat, 2000).
text.formatted: Metacognition can include processes that operate through implicit, non-conceptual signals such as feelings of knowing, fluency, and confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Koriat, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: It can also involve conceptually-driven processes such as explicit instructions that guide the deliberate regulation of mental actions, such as in explicit reasoning or attention training strategies (Jahn et al., 2023; Proust, 2013).
text.formatted: It can also involve conceptually-driven processes such as explicit instructions that guide the deliberate regulation of mental actions, such as in explicit reasoning or attention training strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Jahn et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Proust, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The present account focuses on explicit, conceptually guided mental actions as they provide the starting point for the process of automatization examined below.

Metacognitive monitoring refers to detecting, representing, and evaluating features of one's cognitive and affective states and processes, including their relation to current goals, such as attentional stability, emotional intensity, or memory accuracy.
Metacognitive control refers to regulating these states and processes by deploying mental actions directed toward metacognitive goals.

Mental actions are operations intended to alter or maintain mental activity, such as directing focus, regulating an emotional response, or adopting a particular mode of observation such as transience.

Monitoring and control form a reciprocal loop: monitoring can identify discrepancies between current and intended mental states (e.g., distraction), while control regulates mental activity to reduce those discrepancies (Nelson & Narens, 1990).
text.formatted: Monitoring and control form a reciprocal loop: monitoring can identify discrepancies between current and intended mental states (e.g., distraction), while control regulates mental activity to reduce those discrepancies <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Nelson & Narens, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Metacognitive control is distinguished from cognitive control by the content of the goal toward which control processes are directed (Lange, 2025).
text.formatted: Metacognitive control is distinguished from cognitive control by the content of the goal toward which control processes are directed <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lange, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: On this view, cognitive control regulates mental activity instrumentally in pursuit of a further, usually external goal, such as directing one's focus toward the road while driving.
Metacognitive control takes as its goal some internal mental state or cognitive process, such as stabilizing attention or developing a subtle perception of transience.

While metacognitive goals may also contribute to broader meditative or therapeutic aims, the agent's immediate control processes are directed toward them as proximal goals to be attained in their own right.

Many researchers consider the fundamental psychological capacity that is exercised in meditative practices such as mindfulness to be a form of metacognitive control (Dorjee, 2016; Jankowski & Holas, 2014; Lange, 2025; Repetti, 2022).
text.formatted: Many researchers consider the fundamental psychological capacity that is exercised in meditative practices such as mindfulness to be a form of metacognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dorjee, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jankowski & Holas, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lange, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Repetti, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The relevant goal need not be consciously represented each time a learned procedure is executed.
On the present account, a procedure remains metacognitive insofar as it regulates mental activity toward that goal, even when its execution no longer requires explicit instruction retrieval.
Metacognitive skill refers to the learned capacity to monitor and regulate mental processes reliably and flexibly across contexts in pursuit of metacognitive goals.

Examples include regulating one's own learning (Veenman et al., 2006), deliberately applying formal rules in scientific reasoning (Kuhn, 2000) as well as therapeutic strategies such as cognitive reframing and decentering (Kraft et al., 2026; Zawidzki, 2019).
text.formatted: Examples include regulating one's own learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Veenman et al., 2006)</ref>, deliberately applying formal rules in scientific reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kuhn, 2000)</ref> as well as therapeutic strategies such as cognitive reframing and decentering <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kraft et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Zawidzki, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: During meditation, metacognitive control is directed toward a specialized subset of metacognitive goals such as concentration, equanimity, compassion, and perceptual modes including transience, selflessness, and incongruence.

On this view, advanced meditation is a specialized domain of metacognitive skill, where metacognitive control processes are trained to reliably and flexibly achieve these mental capacities and experiential outcomes.
Section 3 examines a skill-acquisition mechanism through which these control processes improve with practice.
Skills are learned capacities for reliably and flexibly achieving valuable outcomes across varying conditions (Christensen et al., 2019; Fridland, 2019).
text.formatted: Skills are learned capacities for reliably and flexibly achieving valuable outcomes across varying conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Christensen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fridland, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: They encompass a wide range of activities, from everyday language use, reading, and driving to mathematics, chess, and musical performance.
Early theories of skill learning focused on a candidate unifying principle-the gradual automatization of performance through practice.

Since then, skill theorists have broadened their accounts of expert performance, arguing that some aspects of skill never fully automatize and emphasizing a greater role for cognitive control and metacognition (Christensen et al., 2016; Pacherie & Mylopoulos, 2021).
text.formatted: Since then, skill theorists have broadened their accounts of expert performance, arguing that some aspects of skill never fully automatize and emphasizing a greater role for cognitive control and metacognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Christensen et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Pacherie & Mylopoulos, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Given the nascent state of cognitive accounts of meditative skill acquisition, a productive starting point is to examine the knowledge representations and processes of automatization emphasized in classic accounts of skill learning.
These foundational accounts offer a starting point for a broader explanation of meditative expertise that includes flexibility and higher-level control.
A prominent framework characterizes skill automatization as a three-stage progression from deliberate, effortful, instruction-guided action to increasingly fluent and automatic performance.
This stage-based framework was popularized by Fitts and Posner's (1967) theory of perceptual-motor skill and extended by Anderson (1982) to cognitive skill.
text.formatted: This stage-based framework was popularized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fitts and Posner's (1967)</ref> theory of perceptual-motor skill and extended by <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anderson (1982)</ref> to cognitive skill.

text.text: Anderson explains this transition through knowledge compilation, which involves composition and proceduralization.
Composition combines sequences of operations into more unified procedures, while proceduralization embeds declarative information within those procedures, reducing reliance on explicit instructions.
Together, these processes make performance more fluent and efficient.
In this paper, we use automatization as a broader term for this change.
This general account has since been applied to motor, cognitive, and metacognitive skills, with preliminary applications to mindfulness development (Ford et al., 2005; Conway-Smith, 2025; Kee, 2019).
text.formatted: This general account has since been applied to motor, cognitive, and metacognitive skills, with preliminary applications to mindfulness development <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ford et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Conway-Smith, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kee, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We apply this skill-based framework here to propose a cognitive account of how advanced meditative capacities develop and stabilize.

Specifically, we propose that the automatization of metacognitive control helps to explain increasingly effortless and self-sustaining concentration, the development of integrated insight, and the stable capacities associated with meditative endpoints.
This account centers on key information-types used by basic and advanced meditators, specifically explicit, declarative knowledge and implicit, procedural knowledge.
Declarative knowledge is propositionally-structured and consists of consciously accessible facts, rules, and instructions that guide performance.
It is supported by a declarative memory system that depends largely on medial temporal lobe structures, particularly the hippocampus (Squire et al., 2004; Stocco et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It is supported by a declarative memory system that depends largely on medial temporal lobe structures, particularly the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Squire et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Stocco et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, while declarative knowledge may hold instructions for goal-directed action, it does not by itself execute performance.
Instructions are acted out by procedural knowledge, which deploys the specific, goal-directed actions.
In Anderson's framework, procedural knowledge is formatted as condition-action statements that prescribe actions in response to associated cues.
Through repeated practice, procedural knowledge is built, refined, and stored within procedural memory.
Procedural learning relies more heavily on cortico-striatal circuits involving the basal ganglia (Anderson et al., 2008; Doyon & Benali, 2005).
text.formatted: Procedural learning relies more heavily on cortico-striatal circuits involving the basal ganglia <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Doyon & Benali, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Early in learning, agents rely on declarative knowledge, including facts and instructions that guide the appropriate actions toward a goal (e.g., driving a vehicle, playing chess, or directing attention).
Repeated practice builds and refines procedural associations between task conditions and actions, which increasingly guide performance over time.
Broadly speaking, this transition unfolds across three stages of skill acquisition: Basic: Actions are initially guided by declarative knowledge (instructions, facts, and strategies).
Intermediate: Through practice, declarative knowledge is gradually converted into implicit procedural routines that are refined and increasingly automatized.
Advanced: Procedurally guided actions become relatively effortless, fast, effective, and automatic.
One important consequence of automatization is that it reduces demand on working memory (Haith & Krakauer, 2018; Masters, 1992).
text.formatted: One important consequence of automatization is that it reduces demand on working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Haith & Krakauer, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Masters, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Because practitioners no longer need to consciously recall explicit instructions, working memory can be reinvested into higherlevel control functions.
These resources can then be redirected toward the flexible control characteristic of expert skill.
These include monitoring progress, detecting errors, and adapting to changes in internal or external conditions.
In metacognitive skill, this process of automatization concerns the regulation of cognition itself, rather than externally directed behavior.
A basic practitioner may initially rely on explicit knowledge about when and how to monitor or control reasoning, emotion, memory, attention, or other cognitive processes.
Initially, these mental actions are slow, error prone, and effortful.

With repeated practice, metacognitive monitoring and control become increasingly automatized, allowing internal conditions to cue the appropriate metacognitive responses more directly and with less reliance on deliberate instructions.
Through this process, metacognitive control becomes increasingly effective, effortless, and automatically deployed.

Related empirical findings include increasingly efficient emotion regulation following structured practice (Christou-Champi et al., 2015), evidence consistent with automatization of memory retrieval (Racsmány et al., 2018), and improved reasoning following repeated training (Franiatte et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Related empirical findings include increasingly efficient emotion regulation following structured practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Christou-Champi et al., 2015)</ref>, evidence consistent with automatization of memory retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Racsmány et al., 2018)</ref>, and improved reasoning following repeated training <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Franiatte et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support the broader plausibility of practice-related gains in efficiency and automaticity, although they do not all directly test the proceduralization of metacognitive control.

Of particular relevance to meditation, Ramamurthy and Blaser (2017) describe how practice can give rise to "procedural attention," in which learned rules of attentional selection operate automatically, much as procedural memory supports motor skill.

text.text: The same developmental progression has been explored in relation to mindfulness practice. Kee (2019) applies Fitts and Posner's (1967) three-stage framework to mindfulness development, describing a cognitive stage guided by explicit instructions, an associative stage marked by reduced reliance on instructions and greater application across contexts, and an autonomous stage in which mindful attention and nonjudgmental awareness become relatively automatic and effortless.

text.text: However, the proposed transition from instruction-guided to increasingly automatic metacognitive control in meditation remains to be directly tested.
Mindfulness has also been described as a de-automatizing practice that interrupts habitual cognitive and emotional reactions (Kang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Mindfulness has also been described as a de-automatizing practice that interrupts habitual cognitive and emotional reactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This is compatible with the present account because habitual reactions and the metacognitive skills that regulate them can change in different ways.
Habitual emotional reactions can develop unintentionally, without deliberate training, and persist even when maladaptive.
In contrast, the metacognitive skills considered here are deliberately cultivated to improve regulation, becoming increasingly automatic while remaining responsive to conscious adjustment.
Automatization of these self-regulatory skills could therefore help practitioners interrupt habitual maladaptive reactions and respond more flexibly.
The preceding sections have provided the background for treating automatization as a mechanism of skill learning and advanced meditation as a specialized form of metacognitive skill.
Here, we develop this proposal by examining how increasingly automatic metacognitive control may support specific advanced meditative capacities.

ACAM, AIIM, and MEND are represented at the meta-level as domains that organize monitoring and control around particular meditative goals and experiential targets.

Applying this account to meditation requires specifying its phenomenological targets, the mental actions that attain them, and how practice changes their deployment.
Sections 4.2-4.4 will examine this process across the three stages of skill acquisition and its role in advanced concentration, insight, and the flexible integration of meditative capacities.
Advanced meditation practices are directed toward specific phenomenological targets.
Here, we focus on two complementary pathways: ACAM and AIIM.
As summarized in Table 1, these pathways cultivate different experiential capacities while contributing to the broader development of meditative states, stages, and endpoints.

text.text: In AIIM and the Insight Development Process, targets include ways of perceiving experience in terms of transience, selflessness, and incongruence with expectations.
These "perceptual modes" may develop from momentary experiences into increasingly integrated insight (Grabovac et al., 2026; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b).
text.formatted: These "perceptual modes" may develop from momentary experiences into increasingly integrated insight <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Grabovac et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Within the present account, metacognitive monitoring and control are organized toward attaining these phenomenological targets.
A phenomenological target should be distinguished from both the object of practice and the proximal metacognitive goals used to attain it.
For instance, the breath, a visual point, or a bodily sensation may serve as an object of attention.
Sustaining attention on that object, detecting distraction, and returning attention when it wanders are proximal metacognitive goals.
Through practice, more stable attention makes it easier to monitor ongoing mental activity, while metacognitive monitoring and control help sustain attention and restore it when it wanders.
Repeatedly attaining these goals may, in turn, support the development and stabilization of advanced concentrative states.

Similarly, insight practices direct metacognitive activity toward ways of attending to experience that may initially produce momentary and subsequently more integrated perceptions of transience, selflessness, or incongruence.
Table 1 Targets of Advanced Meditation Meditative instructions translate these targets and goals into trainable mental actions.
They consist of declarative knowledge that specifies how cognition should be monitored or controlled.
On our account, repeatedly practicing these actions builds the implicit condition-action associations through which procedural knowledge enacts the instructions.

For example, an explicit instruction such as "when you notice your attention has wandered, disengage from the distraction and return to the breath" identifies both an internal condition and the mental action to be performed.
Insight practices may also instruct practitioners to observe the arising and passing of experience, disengage from conceptual rumination, or maintain a nonreactive mode of observation.
These instructed actions are strategies for attaining the phenomenological target, rather than the target itself.

We use these frameworks to specify the meditative capacities that the proposed learning mechanism may help explain, without assuming that their categories or developmental sequences apply uniformly across traditions or practitioners.
The account's applicability to other descriptions of meditative development remains an empirical question.
During early meditation practice, instructions are typically delivered verbally and held in working memory, so performance depends on explicit guidance and deliberate control.
Through repeated action, the execution of instructions becomes encoded in increasingly task-specific procedures connecting internal conditions with the appropriate mental actions.
For example, detecting a distraction may begin to automatically cue attentional refocusing without needing the instructions to be consciously retrieved.

We propose that, as these explicit strategies become increasingly automatic, meditative control becomes more stable, fluent, and relatively effortless, thereby supporting the development of advanced meditative capacities.
Section 4.2 will map this transition onto the basic, intermediate, and advanced stages of meditative skill.
The development of meditative skill can be organized into three stages corresponding to the general progression described in Section 3.

Whereas the skill-acquisition literature commonly uses the terms novice, intermediate, and expert, we follow the advanced meditation literature in referring to the corresponding stages as basic, intermediate, and advanced.
These labels describe points along a gradual progression rather than sharply distinct phases.
Basic.
Practice initially depends on explicit instructions that specify how attention and other cognitive processes should be monitored and controlled.
Practitioners must retrieve and interpret these instructions while applying them to a meditation object or experiential target.
Performance is therefore relatively slow, effortful, and dependent on working memory.
Intermediate.
With repeated practice, mental actions guided by instructions become increasingly associated with task-specific conditions, allowing them to be acted out more directly.
This transition marks the beginning of automatization.
Relevant internal conditions, such as detecting distraction, begin to cue the appropriate procedural knowledge, which deploys mental actions more rapidly.
This reduces the reliance on explicit instructions and allows meditative control to become faster, more reliable, and less effortful.
The mental actions supporting specific phenomenological targets may begin to arise spontaneously.
Through extensive practice, procedural knowledge can be cued and deployed with minimal conscious deliberation.
The relevant conditions increasingly elicit appropriate monitoring and control operations without requiring the practitioner to retrieve the original instruction.
Meditative performance consequently becomes more fluent, stable, and relatively effortless, while remaining available for strategic adjustment when conditions change.
This account of automatization can be applied to two complementary pathways of advanced meditation: the stabilization of advanced concentrative absorption states and the integration of insight.
Although these pathways involve different phenomenological targets, we propose that both draw on metacognitive strategies that become more reliable, fluent, and less reliant on deliberate control.

In advanced concentrative absorption meditation (ACAM; Sparby & Sacchet, 2024), practitioners repeatedly perform actions such as sustaining attention, detecting distraction, disengaging from competing content, and regulating the intensity of effort.
text.formatted: In advanced concentrative absorption meditation (ACAM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sparby & Sacchet, 2024)</ref>, practitioners repeatedly perform actions such as sustaining attention, detecting distraction, disengaging from competing content, and regulating the intensity of effort.

text.text: As these actions become increasingly automatic, distractions may be detected and corrected more quickly, with less need to retrieve and consciously apply explicit instructions.
This may allow concentrative states to become increasingly stable, effortless, and self-sustaining, supporting progressively deeper absorption.
Importantly, greater stability need not be accompanied by greater subjective intensity.
Jhāna-type advanced concentrative absorption meditation (ACAM-J) comprises eight absorption states, referred to here as J1-J8.

With experience, earlier states of ACAM-J such as J1 and J2 may become more stable and effortless even as their intensity or salience diminishes, a pattern consistent with increasing efficiency and automaticity rather than reduced skill.

In later ACAM-J states, automatization may also support the stability of increasingly subtle contents of consciousness, including minimal expansive spatiality (J5), minimal expansive consciousness (J6), absence perception (J7), and liminality perception (J8).

In advanced investigative insight meditation (AIIM; Grabovac et al., 2026; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b), practice repeatedly directs attention toward specific features of experience and cultivates distinct perceptual modes, including transience, in which phenomena are experienced as arising and passing.
text.formatted: In advanced investigative insight meditation (AIIM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Grabovac et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b)</ref>, practice repeatedly directs attention toward specific features of experience and cultivates distinct perceptual modes, including transience, in which phenomena are experienced as arising and passing.

text.text: Through repetition, strategies for accessing such perceptual modes, disengaging from conceptual rumination, and maintaining nonreactive awareness may become increasingly accessible and stable.

Improved perceptual discrimination and increasingly automatic regulation may make complementary contributions to this development. Conway-Smith and West (2024) propose a computational mechanism linking them: faster and simpler monitoring procedures may increase the likelihood of detecting fleeting or intermittent changes in internal states.
text.formatted: Improved perceptual discrimination and increasingly automatic regulation may make complementary contributions to this development. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Conway-Smith and West (2024)</ref> propose a computational mechanism linking them: faster and simpler monitoring procedures may increase the likelihood of detecting fleeting or intermittent changes in internal states.

text.text: Applied to investigative insight, this could help practitioners notice affective fluctuations that previously went undetected, making their arising and passing more perceptually accessible.
Automatization may also make disengagement from conceptual elaboration and sustained observation less dependent on explicit instructions.
This proposed link between procedural learning and perceptual access remains to be empirically tested, including whether it contributes to the IDP's perceptual modes of selflessness and incongruence.

By enabling more reliable and efficient deployment of the supporting operations, automatization may help initially momentary insights become more integrated into ongoing perception and cognition, and easier to access intentionally even when the corresponding modes are not continuously active (Grabovac et al., 2026; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b).
text.formatted: By enabling more reliable and efficient deployment of the supporting operations, automatization may help initially momentary insights become more integrated into ongoing perception and cognition, and easier to access intentionally even when the corresponding modes are not continuously active <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Grabovac et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Sparby & Sacchet, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Automatization therefore does not determine the content of advanced states or insights.
Instead, it provides a learning mechanism through which the metacognitive operations that support them become sufficiently developed to sustain advanced concentration and integrated insight.
Automatization may support advanced meditation not only by improving individual skills but also by reducing their working-memory demands.
At the basic stage, practitioners must consciously retrieve instructions, monitor performance, and deploy appropriate mental actions.

As these operations become increasingly automatic, they require less deliberate attention, preserving cognitive resources for higher-level monitoring, strategic regulation, and engagement with subtler aspects of experience.
This is particularly important because expertise typically involves a repertoire of actions rather than mastery of a single action (Shepherd, 2021).
text.formatted: This is particularly important because expertise typically involves a repertoire of actions rather than mastery of a single action <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Shepherd, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Reduced working-memory demands may help practitioners coordinate several well-practiced skills concurrently, consistent with evidence that extensive practice can reduce interference between simultaneously performed tasks (Schumacher et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Reduced working-memory demands may help practitioners coordinate several well-practiced skills concurrently, consistent with evidence that extensive practice can reduce interference between simultaneously performed tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Schumacher et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In the emotion-regulation literature, the concurrent use of multiple regulatory strategies is referred to as polyregulation (Ford et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In the emotion-regulation literature, the concurrent use of multiple regulatory strategies is referred to as polyregulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ford et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This may help explain how advanced meditation practitioners can simultaneously coordinate several meditative skills, such as attentional stability, equanimity, effort regulation, and meta-awareness (explicit awareness of one's ongoing mental activity).
When these metacognitive abilities become sufficiently practiced, they may function together rather than as separate strategies that must each be consciously managed.
This may also help explain how advanced practitioners coordinate multiple forms of metacognitive control while maintaining a relatively effortless mode of practice.
Importantly, automatization need not imply rigid or inflexible control.
Skilled procedures remain responsive to context and can be modified as the conditions change.

An experienced practitioner may increase effort when their attention becomes unstable, reduce effort when control becomes excessive, or shift strategies such as increasing equanimity during a surge of emotion.

Greater automatic control may therefore support meditative flexibility by making wellpracticed procedures available while preserving cognitive resources for higher-level monitoring and strategic adjustment.
On this account, meditative expertise involves neither complete conscious control nor entirely automatic performance.
Instead, it involves the flexible integration of increasingly automatic capacities that remain responsive to conscious control.
This account may help explain the combination of spontaneous and consciously guided control that is characteristic of advanced meditation.
The cognitive and experiential changes described previously during skill learning should also be reflected in meditative development.
Our concern here is not the full phenomenology of advanced meditation or the particular contents of advanced states and insights.
Rather, it is how the experience of metacognitive actions changes as those actions become increasingly automatized.

We propose that this development is associated with three broad experiential shifts: from explicit instruction toward fluent engagement; from effortful regulation toward greater stability and integration; and from deliberate control toward a less salient sense of authorship.

Skill acquisition is described by Fitts (1964) and Anderson (1982) primarily in terms of changes in performance and knowledge representation. Dreyfus and Dreyfus (1986) offer a complementary phenomenological account of how the transition toward expertise is experienced.
text.formatted: Skill acquisition is described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Fitts (1964)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anderson (1982)</ref> primarily in terms of changes in performance and knowledge representation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dreyfus and Dreyfus (1986)</ref> offer a complementary phenomenological account of how the transition toward expertise is experienced.

text.text: Their model describes a progression from explicit, context-independent rule-following toward increasingly fluent, intuitive, and context-sensitive engagement.
Although the authors do not specify the cognitive mechanism responsible for this development, they provide a useful phenomenological account of skill learning through various stages.
This progression captures only part of the phenomenology of expertise, as deliberate monitoring and cognitive control continue to play important roles (Christensen et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This progression captures only part of the phenomenology of expertise, as deliberate monitoring and cognitive control continue to play important roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Christensen et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, we focus on the experiential changes associated with automatization, in keeping with the scope of this paper.
Basic meditation may be experienced as a sequence of deliberate and partially separate operations.
Instructions must be recalled, the relevant features of experience identified, and the appropriate mental actions selected.
A practitioner might notice that their attention has wandered, recall the instruction to disengage, and then deliberately return attention to the object of meditation.
Because these operations are not yet well coordinated, practice may feel effortful, intermittent, and unstable.
With practice, internal conditions begin to cue the appropriate responses more directly.
For example, a distraction may increasingly cue attentional refocus, while rumination may cue disengagement, without the practitioner needing to recall the full instruction consciously.
Practice therefore becomes less conceptually dependent and more automatic and fluent.
During the transition from basic to advanced meditation, instances of fluency will alternate with occasions when instructions need to be recalled.
At more advanced levels, monitoring and control may occur quickly and with little conscious deliberation.
Rather than experiencing meditation as separate instances of corrective actions, the practitioner may experience a more continuous and integrated engagement.
The relevant features of one's internal experience become more perceivable, and the appropriate mental actions may arise more rapidly in response to them.
In this way, the intuitive and contextsensitive responses described by Dreyfus and Dreyfus reflect a greater connection between internal conditions and metacognitive actions.
The reduction of effort is one of the clearest experiential results of skill automatization.
A basic meditator must divide their attention between the object of meditation, the instructions for practice, the monitoring of performance, and corrective actions.
As these operations become automatized, they place fewer demands on working memory, and metacognitive control becomes more automatic and spontaneous.
This may help explain the increasing stability and self-sustaining quality of ACAM.

When sustaining one's attention, detecting distraction, and making corrections no longer require constant effort, concentration may be experienced less as something that must be repeatedly restored and more as stable and self-sustaining (Sparby & Sacchet, 2024).
text.formatted: When sustaining one's attention, detecting distraction, and making corrections no longer require constant effort, concentration may be experienced less as something that must be repeatedly restored and more as stable and self-sustaining <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Sparby & Sacchet, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This account may also help to explain the integration of insight.
Early experiences of transience, selflessness, or incongruence may be brief and intermittent.
Their episodic quality may partly reflect the need to deliberately and effortfully initiate a particular mode of perception.
As the supporting metacognitive operations become more fluent, access to these perceptual modes becomes easier, more frequent, and more continuous.
Importantly, automatization concerns changes in the metacognitive actions that support insight, rather than the insights themselves.
Consequently, this account helps to explain the cognitive mechanisms supporting momentary insights and how they become increasingly stable (Grabovac et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Consequently, this account helps to explain the cognitive mechanisms supporting momentary insights and how they become increasingly stable <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Grabovac et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The reduction of cognitive demands also helps account for how several meditative capacities may operate together.
Attentional stability, awareness, equanimity, effort regulation, and compassion may be coordinated and deployed in tandem.
The phenomenology of advanced meditation practice may therefore not only involve a sense of fluency, but also the experience of multiple capacities operating in an integrated way.
Automatization might suggest an apparent paradox: that practitioners may acquire greater control over mental activity while experiencing a less pronounced sense of initiating those actions.

Motor-learning findings suggest that practice can alter agency, although the direction depends on the task and measure. Dempsey-Jones et al. (2023) found reduced intentional binding, an indirect measure associated with agency, following motor practice, whereas van der Wel et al. (2012) found that the sense of agency increased with better performance.

(2023)</ref> found reduced intentional binding, an indirect measure associated with agency, following motor practice, whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">van der Wel et al. (2012)</ref> found that the sense of agency increased with better performance.

text.text: Applied to meditation, the present account proposes that practiced mental actions may require less deliberate initiation, without implying a general reduction in the sense of control.
In contrast, a basic meditator experiences themselves as deliberately directing attention, refocusing from distraction, or altering their mode of perception.
With practice, these actions may occur more spontaneously in response to internal conditions.
Attention returns, effort readjusts, or rumination subsides without being preceded by a conscious intention.

This may help explain how advanced meditation can involve the combination of greater self-regulation abilities along with a sense of effortlessness, spontaneous awareness, and reduced self-related processing (i.e., self-attenuation).
A decreased sense of authorship should not be understood as a lack of conscious awareness or control.
Research on skilled action suggests that expertise can involve remaining continuously sensitive to changing conditions, goals, and the quality of one's performance (Terrien et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Research on skilled action suggests that expertise can involve remaining continuously sensitive to changing conditions, goals, and the quality of one's performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Terrien et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Advanced practitioners can deliberately redirect attention, modify a strategy, or increase effort when internal or external conditions change.
For instance, a skilled tennis or chess player can fluidly modify their strategies based on the performance of their opponent, or their own internal states such as fatigue.
Similarly, an advanced meditator may fluidly adapt their attentional control processes in response to distractions or emotional fluctuations.
Hence, advanced meditative skill is experienced neither as continuous deliberate control nor as entirely unconscious automaticity.
It involves increasingly fluent and relatively effortless metacognitive activity that remains responsive to intentions and changing conditions.
These experiential changes provide a complementary phenomenological account of the automatization of metacognitive control.
The present account describes a learning mechanism through which meditative skill may develop, yet it does not imply that long-term practice alone is sufficient.
The same is true in other skill domains: someone may spend many years writing novels or playing an instrument without attaining literary or musical mastery (Ehmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The same is true in other skill domains: someone may spend many years writing novels or playing an instrument without attaining literary or musical mastery <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Ehmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, advanced meditative skill requires more than the automaticity that may develop through long-term repetition (Galante et al., 2023; Sparby et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, advanced meditative skill requires more than the automaticity that may develop through long-term repetition <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Galante et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sparby et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: An important distinction between long-term and advanced practice may therefore lie in how training is structured, since training conditions shape how effectively metacognitive procedures are acquired and refined.
Drawing on exercise science, Ehmann et al. (2025) provide a framework for describing contemplative training in terms of variables such as volume, duration, frequency, density, and intensity.
text.formatted: Drawing on exercise science, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Ehmann et al. (2025)</ref> provide a framework for describing contemplative training in terms of variables such as volume, duration, frequency, density, and intensity.

text.text: These variables characterize the amount, temporal distribution, and intensity of practice, while programming and periodization concern how training is organized over shorter and longer periods.
Importantly, the framework distinguishes the length of a practitioner's training history from the volume and density of their actual practice.
Practitioners with similar years of experience may therefore have substantially different training histories.
These training variables should be distinguished from the cognitive mechanism proposed here.
While automatization involves changes in the representations governing performance, training variables describe the conditions under which those changes occur.
Greater practice volume may strengthen associative connections between internal conditions and the appropriate mental actions.
However, equivalent amounts of practice may produce different effects depending on how regularly and intensively the actions are performed.
Meditative development should therefore not be understood simply as a function of accumulated practice hours.
Beyond the amount and distribution of practice, feedback may also shape which metacognitive actions are learned and selected.
Work on metacognitive reinforcement learning suggests that actions followed by better outcomes become more likely to be selected again in similar situations (Krueger et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Work on metacognitive reinforcement learning suggests that actions followed by better outcomes become more likely to be selected again in similar situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Krueger et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Comparator mechanisms may support metacognitive monitoring by detecting discrepancies between current cognitive states and metacognitive goals, thereby informing corrective control (Proust, 2013).
text.formatted: Comparator mechanisms may support metacognitive monitoring by detecting discrepancies between current cognitive states and metacognitive goals, thereby informing corrective control <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Proust, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In meditation, for example, a practitioner may aim to sustain attention on an object, notice when the mind has wandered, and redirect attention toward the intended object.
Across repeated practice, actions that more successfully achieve the goal may become more likely to be selected.
Reinforcement learning could complement automatization by influencing which operations are learned and selected, while automatization makes those operations more fluent and less effortful.
Consistent with the principle of training specificity, the effects of meditative training should depend on the particular mental actions practiced and the conditions under which they are performed.
For example, repeatedly observing transience, disengaging from conceptual rumination, and maintaining nonreactive awareness may refine the skills needed for investigative insight.
The sequence in which these skills are learned may also matter.
Developing stable attention, for example, may provide a foundation for subtler practices such as cultivating a perception of transience.
Learning these skills separately may make them easier to coordinate later, which could help explain why many meditative systems develop attentional stability before more advanced forms of insight.
Meditative skill should not be expected to develop smoothly or uniformly.
Research on cognitive skill acquisition suggests that gradual improvement can be interrupted when learners adopt a new strategy (Tenison & Anderson, 2016).
text.formatted: Research on cognitive skill acquisition suggests that gradual improvement can be interrupted when learners adopt a new strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Tenison & Anderson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to meditation, proficiency in a technique may increase gradually, whereas a change in technique, target, or mode of control may temporarily reduce effectiveness.
Development may consequently include periods of improvement, consolidation, plateau, and temporary regression.
When learning a new technique or pursuing a more demanding target, practitioners may return to explicit and effortful control, drawing on skills that are already well established.
An increase in difficulty or perceived effort does not necessarily indicate a loss of skill.
It may reflect the development of a more advanced procedure, or the coordination of multiple capacities.
Meditative development is also likely to be multidimensional (Galante et al., 2023; Murray et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Meditative development is also likely to be multidimensional <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Galante et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Murray et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Changes in different capacities need not occur together.
For instance, a practitioner may gain momentary access to a perceptual mode such as transience before being able to sustain it.
Practitioners may also proceed through separate stages of skill acquisition for different capacities.
Basic, intermediate, and advanced stages should therefore be considered as broad functional descriptions rather than a fixed timetable.
On this account, there is neither a simple relationship between practice hours and expertise nor an identical developmental trajectory for meditative practitioners.
Instead, meditative development entails a complex interaction among the procedural operations being trained, the organization of practice, and the learner's capabilities.
Longitudinal research could test this proposal by investigating how training conditions are associated with changes in fluency, perceived effort, stability, and transfer.
The metacognitive skill acquisition account presented here generates testable predictions that can be examined across neural, behavioral, and phenomenological levels.
No single measure would likely establish the automatization of meditative skill on its own.

Instead, a convergence of evidence is required across several factors, including changes in performance, perceived effort, resistance to interference, and neural recruitment over the course of meditative training.
These predictions can be evaluated by using established methods from skill-acquisition research.
Skill acquisition is associated with well-established changes in the neural systems supporting performance.

Research on motor-skill learning shows that practice reorganizes activity within cortical, striatal, and cerebellar systems, with their contributions varying across learning stages and task types (Doyon & Benali, 2005; Ungerleider et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Research on motor-skill learning shows that practice reorganizes activity within cortical, striatal, and cerebellar systems, with their contributions varying across learning stages and task types <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Doyon & Benali, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Ungerleider et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In a perceptuallearning task, learning to read mirror-reversed text was associated with increased striatal activity and decreased left hippocampal activity (Poldrack & Gabrieli, 2001).
text.formatted: In a perceptuallearning task, learning to read mirror-reversed text was associated with increased striatal activity and decreased left hippocampal activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Poldrack & Gabrieli, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Practice on cognitive tasks has also been associated with reduced recruitment of prefrontal and parietal control regions (Chein & Schneider, 2005).
text.formatted: Practice on cognitive tasks has also been associated with reduced recruitment of prefrontal and parietal control regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chein & Schneider, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Basal ganglia circuits are not limited to motor control.
They are also thought to chunk cognitive action sequences into performance units (Graybiel, 1998).
text.formatted: They are also thought to chunk cognitive action sequences into performance units <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Graybiel, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Internally cued mental actions, such as returning attention to the breath after noticing mind-wandering, could therefore plausibly be chunked in the same way.
If advanced meditation involves the automatization of metacognitive instructions, meditative practice may reveal a parallel neural shift.

Early practice should rely more heavily on neural systems supporting explicit instruction and deliberate control, while skilled practice should involve more efficient and specialized patterns of activity supporting highly stable performance.

Drawing on traditional descriptions of effortless concentration, Lutz et al. (2008) similarly predicted reduced recruitment of attention-regulation systems with extensive practice, interpreting the inverted-U pattern reported by Brefczynski-Lewis et al. (2007) as reflecting neural changes typical of skill acquisition in other domains.

text.text: Longitudinal meditation research provides evidence for changes in attentional stability and its neural correlates.

Following a three-month intensive meditation retreat, Lutz et al. (2009) found a greater reduction in reaction-time variability during an auditory attention task in retreat participants than in a novice comparison group.
text.formatted: Following a three-month intensive meditation retreat, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Lutz et al. (2009)</ref> found a greater reduction in reaction-time variability during an auditory attention task in retreat participants than in a novice comparison group.

text.text: This improvement was associated with increased trial-to-trial consistency of neural responses to attended tones.
These findings support the trainability of attentional stability, although the nonrandomized design limits causal inference and the study did not directly assess dependence on explicit instructions.

Complementary evidence has linked distinct regulatory operations during meditation to neural activity. Hasenkamp et al. (2012) examined breath-focused meditation using practitioners' button presses to identify awareness of mind wandering and estimate surrounding periods of distraction, attentional shifting, and sustained attention.
text.formatted: Complementary evidence has linked distinct regulatory operations during meditation to neural activity. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hasenkamp et al. (2012)</ref> examined breath-focused meditation using practitioners' button presses to identify awareness of mind wandering and estimate surrounding periods of distraction, attentional shifting, and sustained attention.

text.text: Awareness of mind wandering was associated with activity in salience-network regions, whereas shifting and sustaining attention recruited elements of the executive network.
These findings provide neural correlates of the monitoring and control operations central to the present account, but do not establish how those operations become learned or automatized.

This prediction does not imply that advanced meditation becomes exclusively procedural, since deliberate control may still be recruited when practitioners encounter unfamiliar or demanding conditions.
Several measures from the skill-acquisition literature could be adapted to investigate this transition.
Dual-task paradigms could assess how strongly the execution of a meditative skill interferes with a secondary task.
The reduction of interference with training would suggest that the skill requires fewer cognitive resources.

Resistance to disruption could be examined by testing whether capacities such as attentional stability or equanimity remain effective under different conditions such as emotional challenge, fatigue, or environmental distraction.
Subjective workload measures, including the NASA Task Load Index, could provide a complementary measure of reduced cognitive effort.
Repeated measurements across training could also reveal characteristic learning curves.

The proposed account predicts that observable components of meditative performance should improve rapidly during early training and more gradually as skill develops, potentially following the power-law pattern reported in perceptual-motor, cognitive, and attentional skill acquisition (Anderson, 1982; Logan, 1988; Newell & Rosenbloom, 1981; Shin et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The proposed account predicts that observable components of meditative performance should improve rapidly during early training and more gradually as skill develops, potentially following the power-law pattern reported in perceptual-motor, cognitive, and attentional skill acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anderson, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Logan, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Newell & Rosenbloom, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Shin et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, the form and rate of these learning curves may vary across meditative practices depending on the particular skills being trained (e.g., attentional stability, awareness, equanimity, effort regulation, compassion).
Relevant outcomes might include the speed and reliability with which practitioners detect distraction, restore attention, regulate effort, or enter a specific experiential mode.
These improvements should occur alongside reductions in perceived effort and working-memory dependence.
Longitudinal designs would be especially useful because they could distinguish changes produced by training from pre-existing differences between basic and advanced practitioners.

The same developmental pattern may also extend to meta-awareness, with practice enabling practitioners to notice ongoing thoughts as mental events with less effort and less reliance on deliberate monitoring.
This development could be tested by measuring reductions in subjective effort and dual-task interference, while assessing whether the ability to notice ongoing thoughts is maintained or improved.
Improved performance alone would not establish proceduralization.

If practitioners become more proficient at a particular meditative operation but remain equally dependent on explicit instructions and equally susceptible to interference with maintaining those instructions, this would weigh against proceduralization as the explanation for that improvement.
Such tests should compare the same practiced operation under comparable demands, since adopting a new technique or pursuing a more demanding target may renew the need for deliberate control.
For example, longitudinal research could test whether attentional restoration becomes less dependent on maintaining explicit instructions.

This would require establishing that an interference manipulation disrupts instruction maintenance beyond its general attentional demands, and assessing whether any reduction in interference with training exceeds improvement attributable to practice on the secondary task itself.
Researchers should distinguish how often distractions occur from the speed and reliability of restoring attention, while assessing secondary-task performance to account for changes in task priority.
A training-related reduction in instruction-related interference, alongside maintained or improved restoration performance, would support reduced instruction dependence.
Fewer distractions without this change would instead support improved attentional stability as an explanation for reduced effort.
Reduced instruction dependence would be consistent with proceduralization, although it would not uniquely establish knowledge compilation over other learning mechanisms.

To test the proposed contribution to advanced meditation specifically, changes in instruction dependence should be examined alongside independently assessed attainment and stabilization of a specified meditative target, such as a particular absorption state or perceptual mode.
Criteria for that target should be specified separately from the predicted learning signatures, so that reduced effort or automaticity is not itself treated as evidence of advanced attainment.
Behavioral and neural measures can be further complemented by carefully structured first-person reports.
Neurophenomenological approaches examine the dynamic relationships among reported experience, behavior, and neural activity rather than treating any one level as sufficient (Lutz, 2002).
text.formatted: Neurophenomenological approaches examine the dynamic relationships among reported experience, behavior, and neural activity rather than treating any one level as sufficient <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lutz, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Advanced meditators may be especially informative participants because contemplative training can cultivate greater sensitivity to experience and the capacity to reliably enter and sustain specific experiential states across repeated investigations (Berkovich-Ohana et al., 2020; Sacchet & Lieberman, 2026).

text.text: Reports of effort, fluency, stability, verbal mediation, and felt authorship could be collected along with behavioral and neural measures.
The account predicts that increasing skill will be associated with less explicit and effortful regulation, greater experiential continuity, and more spontaneous initiation of metacognitive actions.
A convergence among these first-person changes, behavioral learning signatures, and neural indicators would provide the strongest evidence for the proposed mechanism.
Future research could systematically test this framework longitudinally by examining whether meditative development reliably exhibits the predicted signatures of metacognitive skill acquisition.
These include increasing automaticity, reduced cognitive effort, characteristic learning curves, and measurable changes in neural recruitment.

Research could also determine whether similar patterns occur across the broader meditative activities and experiential domains identified by Sparby et al. (2026), or whether different practices develop through qualitatively distinct learning pathways.

(2026)</ref>, or whether different practices develop through qualitatively distinct learning pathways.

text.text: Automatization may operate alongside other mechanisms of meditative development.
Laukkonen and Slagter (2021), for example, propose that meditation reduces habitual predictive processing, including predictions concerning the self and experiences beyond the present moment.
Active inference models have also formalized meta-awareness and attentional control (Sandved-Smith et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Active inference models have also formalized meta-awareness and attentional control <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Sandved-Smith et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Reviewing applications of active inference to advanced meditation, Tal et al. (2026) identify an increasing emphasis on layer-specific precision re-weighting.
text.formatted: Reviewing applications of active inference to advanced meditation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Tal et al. (2026)</ref> identify an increasing emphasis on layer-specific precision re-weighting.

text.text: The present account complements these approaches by proposing how practice may transform explicitly instructed metacognitive operations into increasingly fluent and automatic procedures.

For example, operations such as disengaging from conceptual elaboration and sustaining nonreactive observation could become increasingly automatic, helping practitioners loosen habitual predictive patterns with less deliberate effort.
On this view, automatizing the regulation of mental activity could support a reduction in habitual processing.

Whether these mechanisms develop together, and whether changes in metacognitive skill contribute to the changes described by predictive-processing accounts, remain questions for empirical investigation.

Future work could further examine meditative skill acquisition in individuals with psychiatric conditions involving altered metacognitive functioning, such as obsessivecompulsive disorder (OCD), and test whether individual differences in confidence, error monitoring, and control affect the observed rate or developmental trajectory of meditative development (Hoven et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2021).

text.text: Another question concerns how metacognitive skills become coordinated with increasing expertise.

A basic meditator may need to perform monitoring, attentional control, and perceptual operations sequentially, whereas advanced practitioners may be able to coordinate several capacities simultaneously or in rapid succession.
Research could examine whether there are limits on coordination and whether some combinations of skills are more seamlessly integrated.
This framework may also help explain the persistent effects associated with meditative endpoints (MEND; Sparby & Sacchet, 2025a).
text.formatted: This framework may also help explain the persistent effects associated with meditative endpoints (MEND; <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sparby & Sacchet, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Studies could investigate whether acquired metacognitive skills contribute to or mediate lasting changes in self-referential processing, affect, cognition, behavior, and well-being following MEND events.
Together, these directions provide a testable research program for investigating how meditative training may produce increasingly stable, integrated, and enduring capacities.
This paper proposes that advanced meditation can be understood, in part, as a specialized domain of metacognitive skill involving the mastery of attentional and perceptual capacities.
Through practice, initially explicit, instruction-guided strategies become increasingly automatic, supporting more efficient, stable, and integrated metacognitive control.
This transition may help explain the stabilization of advanced concentrative states and the integration of insight while preserving flexibility and higher-level strategic control.
Automatization is therefore proposed as a candidate mechanism contributing to meditative development, rather than a complete account of meditative expertise.

By connecting established principles of skill acquisition with neural findings and experiential descriptions, the framework offers a testable cognitive account of how advanced meditative capacities develop.

Clarifying these mechanisms may contribute not only to a deeper scientific understanding of the mind and its capacity for transformation, but also to the development of educational and therapeutic practices that reduce suffering and support human flourishing.
